title: Parallel algebraic surgery for qLDPC codes with constant shuttling depth
authors: Tian-Gang Zhou, Boren Gu, Jens Eisert, Chen Zhao
abstract: Reconfigurable atom arrays provide a promising platform for high-rate quantum low-density parity-check codes, but their computational advantage depends on whether logical operations can be implemented without incurring prohibitive shuttling and space overheads. We introduce algebraic surgery for lifted product codes, co-designing the logical measurements, auxiliary codes, and atom shuttling to enable hardware-efficient Pauli-product measurements. These protocols provide flexible logical addressability subject to the cyclic-symmetry constraint, enabling a broad class of parallel logical measurements, including canonical logical operators with heavily overlapping physical supports and joint measurements within or between code blocks even with different lift sizes, while achieving constant shuttling depth on neutral-atom processors under explicit layout assumptions. In a representative hardware-model benchmark, a cycle supporting 33 parallel canonical logical measurements is about $2\times$ faster than the compared single-observable graph-based surgery schedules, with competitive qubit overhead. These shuttling and circuit-level simulations confirm that the algebraic structure of quantum low-density parity-check codes can be used not only to reduce space overhead, but also to simplify physical implementation and expand the set of efficiently accessible logical operations on neutral-atom processors.
summary: This paper proposes algebraic surgery as a method to efficiently implement logical measurements for qLDPC codes on neutral-atom quantum processors. By leveraging the inherent algebraic structure of the codes, the authors achieve constant shuttling depth and faster cycle times compared to general graph-based approaches. This demonstrates that algebraic insights can simplify physical implementation and expand the accessible logical operations on trapped-atom hardware.
main_problem: The paper addresses the challenge of implementing high-rate quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) codes on physical quantum processors by developing hardware-efficient logical measurement protocols.
main_result: Algebraic surgery provides a method to achieve constant shuttling depth for parallel logical measurements, significantly outperforming general graph-based schedules in simulated cycle times.
method: The authors introduce algebraic surgery, a structured technique applied to lifted product codes, which co-designs logical measurements, auxiliary codes, and atom shuttling to preserve underlying algebraic symmetries.
model_or_system: The physical platform modeled is a reconfigurable atom array using neutral atoms, where connectivity and operations are mediated by controlled atom shuttling via AODs.
key_observables: Shuttling depth ($\delta_{	ext{shuttle}}$), cycle time comparison (algebraic vs. graph-based), Logical Error Rates (LERs), and physical qubit overhead.
important_parameters: The analysis is sensitive to explicit layout assumptions for achieving constant shuttling depth, and performance is benchmarked across varying code sizes and error probabilities ($p$).
main_assumptions: The constant shuttling depth relies on explicit layout assumptions, and the code-capacity results for finite codes do not establish a true error threshold.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the cyclic LP code structure and the comparison of shuttling depths between algebraic and graph-based surgeries. Figure 3 compares shuttling and gate times for syndrome extraction across different code types.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from defining the need for hardware-efficient logical operations to introducing algebraic surgery, benchmarking its performance against existing graph-based methods in terms of time and depth, and finally analyzing the resulting code capacity and error rates.
why_interesting: This work directly tackles the physical realization bottleneck in quantum computation by showing how abstract algebraic structures can be mapped onto physical hardware constraints (like shuttling depth) in a computationally efficient manner.
